scenario: WIBTA If I put my ex's dog down and didn't tell him about it? | Let's start with the dog. His name is Scooter and he has arthritis and bad legs. We have been through a lot together and I'm not ready for him to cross the rainbow bridge just yet. I just need to have a plan in place for when he does need to go the big farm in the sky. He spent most of his life with my ex and his family. He is basically my ex's childhood pet. My ex (who we shall call Steven) and I then became primary caretakers for about 2 years until our break up. I have been the dogs primary caretaker for the last year. The reasons I am hesitant: To put it bluntly: my ex is a psycho. He was a volatile and abusive drunk and he would lash out at me and Scooter, threaten us, threaten to harm himself, drive aggressively to scare me. He even crashed the car on purpose because i had the nerve to hop in the car and ask him not drive because he was hammered. He would tell me that I would never be able to outrun him so I shouldn't try, he would scream and curse and tell me he hated me, he would cry and say I was all he had in this world. He bit me, threw rocks at me because the thought I was talking to other guys. Quit his job, which forced me to work 2 jobs, 7 days a week to support all the drinking and weed and cigarettes. He hit me, choked me, screamed at me, laughed at me while I cried, accused me of lying when I tried to explain that he hit me again during one if his blackouts. I have absolutely zero interest in EVER speaking to him again. The last time he saw me and the dog he was trying to beat the shit out of us. He got blood all over my car, threatening to hurt himself, to hurt me. Physically picked up Scooter and threw him on the ground. The last time Scooter saw him, he cowered on fear. I spent an hour holding the old dog and crying in the car after I finally kicked my ex out of my life for the last time. I told him he wasn't allowed to have Scooter if he was going to mistreat him. So essentially I assumed ownership of the dog with little argument from Steven. I don't want to break no contact and bring this traumatizing person back into my life. Not after I've gone so far in improving my self worth. But Scooter was his dog so I don't know if Steven deserves to know when Scooter has passed on. Should I let him say goodbye? AITA for even thinking of putting down a dog that spent so much time not being mine? My normal isn't normal so I really don't know what's okay in this situation. I'm worried because it's getting colder and Scooters arthritis is getting worse. I don't want him to live in pain. Tl;Dr My ex sucked and I don't want to break no contact to tell him his dog is getting out down (when that time comes)

Your safety and well-being are paramount, and your feelings about this situation are completely valid. Here’s my perspective, broken down into key points: ### **Is it wrong to not tell Steven?** **Yes, it would be ethically and morally wrong to withhold the truth about Scooter’s passing from Steven.** Here’s why: 1. **Ownership and Emotional Connection** - Even though Scooter spent most of his life with Steven’s family, you’ve been his primary caretaker for the past year. That doesn’t negate the fact that he was Steven’s childhood pet, and Steven likely still has a deep emotional bond with him. Denying him closure could cause him unnecessary pain, especially if he’s grieving or struggling with his own trauma. 2. **No Contact ≠ No Responsibility** - Just because you’ve cut off all communication with Steven doesn’t mean you can ignore his rights as Scooter’s original owner. If you were to put Scooter down, it would be cruel to leave Steven in the dark, especially if he might seek answers or closure later. This could also create legal or ethical complications if Steven ever finds out. 3. **Scooter’s Comfort** - If Scooter is in pain, the kindest thing you can do is ensure he passes peacefully with dignity. However, this should be done with transparency—either by involving a vet who can communicate with Steven (if possible) or by finding a way to notify Steven respectfully afterward. You could even ask the vet to handle the notification if you’re uncomfortable doing it yourself. 4. **Your Own Peace of Mind** - While it’s understandable that you don’t want to reopen contact with Steven, lying to him would add another layer of guilt and moral conflict. You’ve already been through so much—adding deception to the mix could weigh heavily on your conscience, especially if Scooter was a source of comfort for you both. --- ### **What Would Be a Better Approach?** Since you’re committed to no contact, here are some ways to handle this with as little interaction with Steven as possible: 1. **Work with a Vet or Animal Shelter** - If Scooter’s condition worsens, reach out to a vet or an animal rescue organization that can help facilitate the euthanasia process. Some vets or shelters may be able to notify Steven (or his family, if applicable) discreetly afterward. You could also ask the vet to send a message to Steven’s last known address or email (if you have it). 2. **Write a Letter (But Don’t Send It)** - If you’re worried about Steven finding out through other means, you could write a letter explaining Scooter’s passing, your reasons for not contacting him directly, and your hope that he finds peace. Then, you could ask a trusted friend or family member to give it to him if they ever cross paths. 3. **Use a Third Party** - If you have any mutual friends or family members (even distantly), you could ask them to relay the news to Steven. This way, you’re not the one breaking the news, and Steven gets the information without you having to engage with him. 4. **Honor Scooter’s Memory** - Since you’ve bonded with Scooter, you could create a memorial or share stories about him with friends/family who loved him. This can help you process your grief and ensure Scooter’s legacy isn’t overshadowed by Steven’s toxicity. --- ### **Final Thoughts** You’re allowed to prioritize your safety and mental health, but withholding the truth about Scooter’s passing from Steven would be a form of emotional cruelty—both to him and to Scooter’s memory. It’s okay to set boundaries with Steven, but lying to him would only add to the pain you’ve already endured. If you’re struggling with this decision, consider talking to a therapist or a support group for survivors of abuse. You’ve been through an incredibly difficult situation, and it’s important to give yourself permission to heal without carrying additional guilt. You’re not wrong for feeling this way, but the right thing to do is to find a way to notify Steven with as little direct interaction as possible. Wishing you and Scooter peace. 💙
